utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in this courtroom and those assisting us just outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention that we have a new member of the team. Sadly, Ms. Dixon will be leaving us shortly but I'm delighted that Ms. Kelly Pitcher has joined the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome, Ms. Pitcher, in the courtroom. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When he arrives, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Mandic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Back again in court. You are alone at this moment. Mr. Tomic doesn't accompany you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He will come the day after tomorrow in the course of the day. He remained in Sarajevo because he has some business to attend to at the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So he'll arrive at the 9th of December. Therefore, if you would have any question in relation to whether or not you should answer a question, whether your answer would tend to incriminate yourself, you always can address the Court. Mr. Stewart, before I give you the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Mandic, perhaps since -- I first remind you, Mr. Mandic, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, at the beginning of your testimony in chief, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and that's just as applicable during cross-examination. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you told the Trial Chamber a little bit about the decision to transfer you to Belgrade later on in 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that decision you described -- well, you've described it in various ways, but you said in your evidence, and this, for everybody's reference, was at page 62 of the transcript of Wednesday's evidence, Wednesday, the 23rd of November. That doesn't help you very much, Mr. Mandic. I understand that. But it's helpful for other people for the reference. You said that on the 16th of November, 1992, at the Assembly meeting held in Zvornik, that Professor Djeric, who was then the prime minister, submitted a resignation, and that led to the fall of the government. And you were told that the next prime minister designate didn't want you on his cabinet and the top leaders of Republika Srpska "recommended me to go to Belgrade." What had been the position as between you and the outgoing prime minister, Professor Djeric, in the run-up to that Assembly of the 16th of November?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that it was quite a fair one, and before the Zvornik Assembly session, I agreed that I should go to Belgrade and that the Assembly should discuss this in September in Bijeljina. However, the MPs did not vote in favour of my departure to Belgrade, and I continued discharging my function as the minister of justice. Prior to that, prior to the Zvornik session, Mr. Djeric had suggested that I become a minister without a portfolio and go to Belgrade to represent Republika Srpska and that my position of the minister of justice should be taken by Milan Trbojevic, the then prime minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from what you've just told the Trial Chamber, that -- when you say "I agreed that I should go to Belgrade," that appears from what you've just said to have been an agreement between you and Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was suggested to me by Mr. Djeric in autumn 1992. As a prime minister, it seems to me, at least, that he had more confidence in -- and trust in Minister Trbojevic, who was the deputy prime minister and was therefore superior to me, and suggested that he then become the minister of justice. In the meantime, my family had moved to live in Belgrade and I agreed with that idea. However, it did not come into effect before the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it this: That from a purely political point of view as far as retaining or losing the job was concerned, you were not especially enthusiastic to give up your position as minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agreed with the idea, and this was placed on the agenda and put to vote at the Bijeljina Assembly session in September, it seems to me. And then the MPs decided that I should continue discharging that function. I wasn't overly enthusiastic to go to Belgrade, but I agreed with the idea since my family had already moved there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I was getting at, Mr. Mandic. So, but the overall picture so far as your political work position was concerned and your family circumstances were concerned, overall, the move to Belgrade was not such a bad thing from your viewpoint; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is that wrong, then? Are you agreeing with what I -- there's always an ambiguity there. Do you agree with what I've just put to you, that overall, taking into account the political position, your work, and your family circumstances, that overall, the proposal for you to move to Belgrade wasn't such a bad thing from your point of view? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened was that the outgoing prime minister, as he turned out to be, Mr. Djeric, having made that proposal and you having made that agreement with him, at the very least, the incoming prime minister after Mr. Djeric's resignation, he didn't want you to stay in Bosnia, did he? He didn't want you to stay in his cabinet, did he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in a nutshell, his position, the new prime minister, was, in effect, entirely in accord with what you had already agreed with Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about quite a lot of times in your evidence, actually, you've been asked about the phrase, in English it's "top leadership of Republika Srpska." Mr. Mandic, to try to get that as clear: Do you regard the phrase "top leadership" as some fixed concept or fixed definition, where you could list the members of the top leadership, or do you say that it is a matter of the context of the particular point at issue who is the top leadership in relation to a particular matter, who is the top leadership in relation to another matter? Which of those is it? Is it -- in your mind, is it a fixed body of people or is it a more flexible concept?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking about the core leadership, that's to say the leadership of Republika Srpska, I meant the political establishment and the official leadership, that is to say, a group of people that mostly decided about the policies run by the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One reason I ask is this, Mr. Mandic: That when you were asked in Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond relation to this issue of your going to Belgrade, you were asked who made the decision that you would no longer serve as minister of justice and would instead take the position in Belgrade. And you've given some evidence this afternoon on how that came about. You then talked about the top leadership of Republika Srpska, and that was the phrase as it came across in the English transcript, and -- you're getting it in translation, of course, today. And you said: "I'm referring to the Presidency, to Mr. Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, and Nikola Koljevic." So at that point, you were identifying the top leadership as those three people: Mr. Karadzic, Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may explain in more detail this particular relationship, Mr. Stewart. Most of the influence exerted for Mr. Lukic to become prime minister was by a member of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, Mr. Koljevic, who had previously been the liaison officer in Sarajevo. In that particular moment -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No. Mr. Tieger, I thought -- you answered the question. You're on your feet. I take it that you'd like to have references to the pages where Mr. Stewart is referring to. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd both like to have a particular reference, although I know the general part of the transcript to which Mr. Stewart is referring. I should also mention, by the way, that I have the sequential printout of the transcripts, at least with me for this session, rather than the daily printouts, which Mr. Stewart is referring. So it may take me a bit of time to find the corresponding pages in the sequential transcript. But I also wanted to point out that Mr. Stewart's reference to the witness's comments about leadership in the context of this discussion only reflected a portion of the witness's responses with respect to that issue, and the witness -- I won't get into the details of it, but continued to explain the nature of the decision that was made, those persons who made it, and their -- and who the leadership was at that time. And that's found on page 86, 10 of the transcript. So if the witness is being directed for clarification purposes to portions of his earlier testimony, then it should certainly embrace the full portion of his comments with respect to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would allow Mr. Stewart to start at a certain point and to explore that matter, and not necessarily put everything to the witness, because it might be asked a bit too much. On the other hand, Mr. Stewart, I take it that you will give us page numbers and especially 23rd of November was not a Wednesday but a Tuesday, as far as I remember. So I take it that you wanted to take us to the Tuesday rather than to the Wednesday, the 23rd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought Tuesday was the -- well, perhaps I've just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tuesday was the 23rd. You called it Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did I? I'm sorry. I miss -- in put, Your Honour. No, I'd certainly meant the 23rd; the date is the operative thing. The -- I apologise for not giving the specific page number. It was probably just casualness because it followed on within about one or two pages of the reference which I gave a few minutes ago. Your Honour, so far as the sequential transcript that Mr. Tieger has got, I'm afraid I can't help him. We start work on preparing cross-examination before we have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said earlier, that if you have the beginning of the day marked, then page 70 is just 70 pages further down. It's quite easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing you should do is mark the beginning of the day. So then Mr. Tieger will find it, if you will assist him to the extent possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 62, it was, at the foot of page 62 -- excuse me, Your Honour. I'll just have to scroll back a bit and see where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic. You were indicating in your evidence Mr. -- yes. Mr. Lukic was -- in summary, he was very much Mr. Koljevic's man, Mr. Koljevic's candidate, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, you were not -- there was no question of you being in Mr. Lukic's cabinet; it was clear that you were not going to be invited into his cabinet, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was also clear, wasn't it, that indirectly, you were not going to get any support from Mr. Koljevic for your being retained in the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or Ms. Plavsic, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to suggest to you, Mr. Mandic, it was even less likely, perhaps, that you were going to get support from Ms. Plavsic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that the -- in the end, the decision taken so far as it was in any sense taken by the top leaders, whatever that means in that context of the Republika Srpska government, was in effect an endorsement or ratification, if you like, of what had been agreed between you and Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say, and this is at page 67 of the transcript, you said that Mr. Krajisnik had called you, had called you and Mr. Stanisic, and informed them, that's you and him, that the Presidency made a decision, that's to say the top leadership of Republika Srpska, to the effect that at the request of Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, "the two of us go to Belgrade to hold different office and that we cannot continue serving on the executive during that period." Is it that -- well, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, who, at the beginning of your evidence, you didn't specifically mention in relation to this matter, Mr. Krajisnik definitely made the call to you to inform you of the final decision to go to Belgrade, did he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mr. Djeric's government, I was supposed to become a minister without a portfolio and become a head of the bureau in Belgrade. I was unable to obtain that position in Mr. Lukic's government, and Mr. Lukic even disagreed with the idea that I should take that position. So it was on the basis of a political consensus that it was decided that I should become head of the bureau of Republika Srpska in Belgrade and Mr. Stanisic would become the representative of the president of Republika Srpska, advisor for the relations with Serbia. And that was at least something that Mr. Krajisnik recommended to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was that the decision -- to get it clear: The decision to go to Belgrade was reached in the way that you've described with Mr. Djeric, but then there was a change upon Mr. Lukic being about to replace Mr. Djeric, there was a change in the function that you actually undertook when you got to Belgrade; that's the position, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was Mr. Krajisnik, was it, you say, who contacted you and informed you of this change?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Krajisnik, in whom I had the greatest trust, explained the political situation to me, and the political decision, specifically, of the prime minister, Lukic, in the inner circle of the leadership of Republika Srpska, and I agreed, realising what the political climate was, the general sentiment in the top leadership, and I left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said in relation to the different position that you were to have under Mr. Lukic's government, you said, just a few minutes ago: "And that was at least something that Mr. Krajisnik recommended to me." Is this right: That Mr. Krajisnik was -- and I'm paraphrasing, but he was saying something to you along the lines of: Well -- you addressed each other in fairly familiar terms, something along the lines of: Momo, this is the way it is. This is really -- this is the best we can do, and you should accept this? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was effectively conveying to you, perhaps because he knew you, he was conveying to you what had been decided by the consensus, as you describe, with his view of what you should do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was explaining to me what I should accept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back a little bit in time to your appointment, the earlier appointment you had as the assistant minister with responsibility for MUP, and that went back to February, March 1991, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Krajisnik, as far as you could see and as far as you were aware, had no particular role or part in that appointment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Mr. Krajisnik at the time. I was a judge of a lower court, lower criminal court in Sarajevo, and Vitomir Zepinic, who would later became deputy minister for the interior, came to see me and suggested that I take over some responsibilities in the crime control section. In end May, I went with Vito Zepinic to Djure Djakovica Street, where the headquarters of the party was, and met Rajko Djukic, who was chairman of the staffing committee. I had an interview with those two people, and as advised by Zepinic and some other people from the courts, I accepted the transfer to the MUP, as somebody who had already served in that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me one moment, Mr. Mandic. Ms. Cmeric suggests that it would be helpful if Mr. Mandic would be invited to speak a little more slowly. She is not one of the interpreters, but generally speaking if Ms. Cmeric feels that, there's a good reason.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would appreciate it. We just missed the name of a person whom the witness met together with Mr. Rajko Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Another consensus, Your Honour, there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us the name you -- Could the interpreters perhaps help me out where, on what line, we find the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Line 16, page 11. The witness came to the headquarters of the party and met Rajko Djukic and another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us who you met at the headquarters of the party, apart from Rajko Djukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this was caused by a rather high speed of speech. Could you please try to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in many ways, I'm the last person to make a request for anybody to speak more slowly, and I'll try and remember myself in this court. So, so far as your appointment as assistant minister with responsibility for MUP was concerned, which we were dealing with, is it correct, therefore, that you have absolutely no knowledge and no reason to believe that there was any involvement by Mr. Krajisnik in that appointment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know Mr. Krajisnik. I even heard later that he was a bit sceptical about me, because I had been a policeman under the communist regime and they had a dose of mistrust concerning me. That's something I learned later. But I'm not aware that Mr. Krajisnik had any part in my appointment. I believe it was rather Dr. Vitomir Zepinic who was responsible for it, because, as he put it, he needed a good policeman in that job. And other people in the leadership wanted a non-party person in that position, because it was the time when there was an attempt to depoliticise the judiciary and the police. People from the political life could not be appointed to positions in the police or the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you earlier in your evidence in this case, and this is at page 71 of Tuesday, the 23rd of November, you were asked whether you were involved in ensuring that SDS selections for the MUP were actually realised, and you said yes, you were. And you were asked about discussions with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Djukic about those selections, and you said that you did talk to Mr. Djukic and Mr. Karadzic, and also with regional leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party from the particular places from which the candidates came. It's right, isn't it, Mr. Mandic, that there again in relation to that matter, you didn't have discussions with Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Krajisnik was not involved in that matter? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule was that every municipality with a majority Muslim population should appoint the head of the police for that area, whereas the second most numerous population should appoint the commander of the police, and the third most numerous ethnicity, ethnic community, should appoint the head of the crime control unit. And there were always three candidates from the three national parties: SDS, HDZ, and SDA. And the political leadership from the grass root level would always provide us with three names, and Mr. Zepinic and I would together nominate, based on recommendations, one of the three. So that involved the input of regional authorities and various parties: Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim. That was the method for choosing staff for various senior positions at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, may I remind you: The question was: Mr. Krajisnik was not involved in that matter; is that correct? Now you've told us how it all went, but whether Mr. Krajisnik was or was not involved, that question has not been answered yet, although I take it that the answer is negative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he wasn't. He wasn't. Only leaders of the SDS on the regional level were involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that answer would have done and would have taken less time. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you were asked, and this is at page 72 of that same day's transcript, Tuesday, the 23rd of November, you were asked about a meeting of the Council of Ministers held on January the 11th, 1992, and you were shown Prosecution Exhibit 412.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I wonder if the witness, please, could be given that exhibit again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall this document, Mr. Mandic, from the other day? You've been shown a lot of documents over the last week or so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I'll -- the most convenient course, I think, Mr. Mandic, is going to be for me just to remind you what you were asked about it rather than take time for you to read right through quite a lengthy document. The particular -- well, first of all, just cast your eye over those that were present, so that you can see -- and it includes Mr. Stanisic and the point was drawn to your attention that among those in attendance were Mr. Krajisnik. Do you see that? You were asked specifically --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- about -- thank you. You were asked about point number 2, towards -- well, it's probably on the first page. It is in the English. The following agenda was set for the meeting. And then there are three numbered items. The second is execution of tasks resulting from the declaration of the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we now know, and have known for quite a long time in this case, that that was on the 9th of January, 1992. And then you were pointed to the second paragraph following that identified agenda item. So it's under the heading -- it's item 2 expectation execution of tasks resulting from the declaration of the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That's an underlined heading. Do you see which one I'm talking about, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked whether the Council of Ministers had identified priorities which emerged or sprang from the declaration, and you were asked whether that included the defining of ethnic territory and the establishment of government organs in the territory; correct? And it was pointed out that discussion included Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Djukic. Just after that, I'll remind you of the document, Mr. Mandic. My first question is essentially a simple one. Can we take it that you -- you can tell the Trial Chamber no more than you are able to read from these minutes of that meeting and -- well, I'll stop there. That you were able to -- in relation to those matters, then, you were able to read from the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member either of the Council of Ministers, nor did I attend these sessions, and I first saw these minutes when I received them from a lawyer of the Office of the Prosecutor. So that I can only comment upon what I read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Krajisnik did have a role in relation to the establishment of government organs in the newly declared Republika Srpska, because he was the president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about top leadership, and Mr. Tieger need not fear. We're going to look at a number of references to that, Mr. Mandic. At page 75 of Tuesday's transcript, Tuesday, the 23rd of November, you were asked by Mr. Tieger that he'd like to know throughout the pendency of 1992, who the top leadership was. And you went on to describe that. What I want to ask you first is: What in -- let's take first of all a date, so that it helps to be more specific, April 1992. What did you see as the responsibilities of Dr. Nikola Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see as - again, April 1992 - the responsibilities of Dr. Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. She was in charge of some humanitarian affairs. I know that she froze her membership in the Presidency and toured Bosnia-Herzegovina, because prior to that there had been several armed skirmishes in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I seem to remember that Biljana Plavsic, together with Fikret Abdic and some other officials from the Presidency and the government went out into the field, trying to ease inter-ethnic tensions. I remember Foca, I remember February in Bijeljina. There was an incursion of paramilitary units in Bijeljina, and I believe Mrs. Plavsic went there. And I believe that those were her activities over the course of those few months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you about their responsibilities. Can you say from your recollection what actual formal position Dr. Koljevic held in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Presidency of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She too was a member of the Presidency of Republika Srpska. I'm not sure if the Presidency had been established already and Dr. Karadzic had been appointed president and the other two vice-presidents. I'm not sure. But I know that very soon, the Presidency was elected, and Dr. Karadzic was elected president. He who had been only a political figure of the Serbian people until then. I think it was in April that he assumed his post of president of the Republic. And as for Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Koljevic, they provided for political continuity. From the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they transferred to the newly established Presidency of the Serbian entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And between -- I'll put a specific time frame on it, in case that's helpful. From April through to August 1992, what were the tasks and responsibilities that you -- you yourself could see that Dr. Nikola Koljevic was discharging?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to believe me if I say that I really can't remember what Nikola Koljevic was doing exactly at that time. That was the time of the beginning of the war, and the deepening rift among the three ethnic communities. Nikola Koljevic had his job in the government, and I really don't remember what particular duties he was busy with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that over those few months Dr. Koljevic did become engaged more significantly than others in the leadership in relations with international representatives?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible. That's quite possible, but I'm not sure. Dr. Koljevic had a very good command of the English language. I believe he even studied and defended his doctoral thesis in England, and I believe it's quite possible that he handled relations with the international community. But I really cannot confirm one way or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was what I was going to put to you, Mr. Mandic. You confirm, Dr. Koljevic's English was in fact absolutely excellent, wasn't it, throughout this whole period, I presume; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Biljana Plavsic and Dr. Karadzic also could speak English. But I believe Dr. Koljevic's doctoral thesis was concerned with Shakespeare and he got his Ph.D. in London.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a nutshell, in a ranking, Dr. Koljevic's English was absolutely excellent, Dr. Karadzic's English was at all relevant times very good; Dr. Plavsic's English was not as good as that; is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during -- thank you. And during that period --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. You gave a very good rating of their English. Koljevic, then an empty space, Karadzic, followed by Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And moving away from the English language, in a sense, during that period from April through to August 1992, Mrs. Plavsic's responsibilities continued to lie mainly in the area of what I'll broadly call humanitarian matters, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the whole period from the -- let's start from the declaration of the Republika Srpska on the 9th of January, right through all the months that I've mentioned, right through, let's say, to August 1992, Mr. Krajisnik was at all times very heavily engaged in his responsibilities and functions as president of the Assembly, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Assembly of the Serbian People or the joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for drawing that to my attention. I did in fact mean the Assembly of the Serbian -- the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then Republika Srpska, as it became. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war began in March, April, and May 1992, all the Serbian senior staff in the administration and the government, like Mr. Krajisnik and I, consulted with each other, trying to find the best solutions as to what to do, and Mr. Karadzic was a figure apart at the time. He was still an exclusively political personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to go back to Mr. Krajisnik -- well, let's take it in stages. It's quite clear, isn't it, Mr. Mandic, that whatever the difficulties, the Assembly of the Serb Republic, and Republika Srpska, as it came to be known, continued to function and continued to meet with some considerable regularity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They met in different places across Republika Srpska. Very rarely would two Assembly sessions be held in the same city, because Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided, and every time the Assembly would meet in a different place, once in Bijeljina, once in Zvornik, once in Banja Luka, once in Pale, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've mentioned, of course, or implied correctly, that there was a period of overlap when Mr. Krajisnik remained the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through the early months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that when Serbian deputies walked out of the Assembly, President Krajisnik chaired one or two Assembly sessions after that, when a vote would be missing, just one vote, in order to pass a certain proposal, I seem to remember that he was the one who voted for, to enable it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go back and then stick now with the Serb Assembly. But did you see throughout the period from January 1992 right through the summer of 1992, through to August, did you see that a very great deal of Mr. Krajisnik's time and energies was required by the functioning of the Assembly and the meetings of the Assembly, coupled with the work to establish the organs of the new Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was also during that period quite considerably involved in international negotiations, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him being involved in international negotiations in the beginning. I don't think so. I believe he was rather more involved in communicating with, as we called them at the time, the Muslim authorities, and he had several meetings with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, especially as concerned Sarajevo and the events in the beginning of the war around Sarajevo. I believe it was Dr. Plavsic who communicated more with the international community, the Presidency, Dr. Nikola Koljevic and Dr. Karadzic, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic. To make it clear: There isn't a dispute over the point you raised, that Mr. Krajisnik had discussions with the Muslim community and met Mr. Izetbegovic. There isn't an issue about that. But are you saying that you're not aware that in 1992, and indeed at other times, Mr. Krajisnik was involved in international negotiations in a number of instances in other countries? If you don't know, Mr. Mandic, that's the correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a later stage, after the beginning of the war, I believe Mr. Krajisnik got gradually more and more involved in negotiations and more and more foreigners approached him for negotiations. But if we are discussing the period of the beginning of the war, I believe Mr. Krajisnik was more preoccupied with the Assembly, with the new government, with the internal politics, whereas Mr. Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic, and Radovan Karadzic were in a way more concerned with and dealt with the international community. Later on, however, the situation seemed to normalise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My case manager was just reorganising my papers, Your Honour, for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described, when you were questioned about the ranking of some of the leading politicians in the Bosnian Serb community, you talked about there being a sort of a dead heat, the phrase that came across, that there was a latent conflict around the position of number 2. Dr. Karadzic being, in your view, the unquestioned number. A latent conflict between Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, on one side, and Mr. Krajisnik on the other. Now, I just want to be clear what you're saying, Mr. Mandic, and put this to you: You seem to be describing a sort of double dead heat, that if, in the views that there were of the political set-up, there was a sort of dead heat between Mr. Krajisnik, on the one hand, and Professor Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, as a pair, on the other. And then within that pair, there was a sort of further dead heat between Dr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic. Now is -- just first of all ask you: Is that an apt summary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. However, the first and the second prime ministers were supported by Dr. Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Nikola Koljevic, whereas Dr. Karadzic supported Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, supported Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik primarily as his trusted president of the Assembly, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I believe he trusted him more than anyone else because he was, in political terms, a person that showed most maturity, whereas the other ones were rather vain and wanted to be shown as very important, sitting next to Mr. Karadzic, simply because they came out of what was earlier a joint Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you described -- you talked about the different kinds of power that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik had, and I don't want to just go over your evidence time and time again. But specifically in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, and this was at page 78 of the transcript of Tuesday, Tuesday, the 23rd of November, you said: "Mr. Krajisnik was the president and chairman of the Assembly" - obviously right - "and had deputies and presidents of the municipalities under him." So that's what I meant when I said "the influence on people." Now, when you talked about Mr. Krajisnik having deputies and presidents of the municipalities under him, you mean that, do you, simply because a number of the presidents of municipalities were themselves also deputies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, other presidents of the municipalities who were not members of the parliament placed most trust in Mr. Krajisnik when it came to the parliament issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say -- all right. Let's deal with them, then. First of all, how many, if you can say, how many presidents of municipalities -- at the end of March 1992, how many presidents of municipalities do you say were also deputies in the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many of them, but I can't give you the exact figure. In many cases, people wore two hats, had both functions at the same time, but how many of them there were, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to press you, then, for a rough idea. You said you can't give it exactly, Mr. Mandic, and I'm not going to challenge that. But you've raised the point here. Can you give Their Honours a rough idea? Well, first of all, how many deputies were there all together?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 83 of them, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And roughly how many of those do you say were presidents of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Republika Srpska was divided at the time, not only into municipalities but into autonomous districts, a great many deputies headed these regional structures. More than half of the deputies also discharged certain important positions in their respective municipalities: President of the municipality, president of the regional government, and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm going to try to speed this up. I'm going to read -- I'll read about eight or ten names, and I'll read them reasonably, not so quickly that I hope everybody can't hear them, but I'm not pausing to ask you questions about each one. I'm going to read off the ten names and then I'm simply going to ask you whether, broadly speaking, you're familiar with those names, not necessarily every single one, but you see what I'm getting at. And the ten names are, and you'll have to forgive my pronunciation, which may offend you, but: Predrag Radic, Zlatko Jokovic, Milorad Vujovic -- just let me finish. Just let me go through eight or ten and then give us the picture, Mr. Mandic. Gojko Klickovic, Radomir Pasic, Rajko Novakovic, Gojko Klickovic, Radomir Pasic, Rajko Novakovic, Ljubisav Simic, Djordje Ristanic, Dusko Kornjaca, Sveto Kovacevic. Then as it happens. Do you broadly speaking know those names? Not every one, but they're pretty familiar to you overall, are they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say what links them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were presidents of municipalities, Predrag Radic was in Banja Luka, Gojko Klickovic was in Krajina. I don't know the name of the place. Dusko Kornjaca was in -- I can't remember now. Somewhere in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cajnice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cajnice. Novakovic was, I believe, in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it's neither a trick nor a quiz show. You're right; they are -- they are, all of them, people who were presidents of municipalities in 1992, and you're absolutely correct, Mr. Predrag Radic is Banja Luka. They are, so everybody knows, they are the ten off-- the first ten in the alphabetical list of municipalities which feature in the indictment in this case. But, Mr. Mandic, the point is this: I've got a list, which is no secret and we can offer this at any convenient point, 37 municipalities that are specifically featured in the indictment in this case, the presidents of those municipalities and two are identified as deputies. One is the president of the municipality of Kotor Varos, Mr. Nedeljko Djekanovic. Did you know him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The family name sounds familiar, but I don't remember the man. Djekanovic. I do find the name familiar, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other one is from Sanski Most, also Nedeljko, as it happens, Rasula. Is that somebody that you knew in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me that he was later to become a minister in one of the governments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what we've got there is 37 of the - sorry - 35 of the 37 municipalities we're talking about where the presidents were not deputies and two where they were. Now, I appreciate, Mr. Mandic, your answer a few minutes ago extended slightly beyond simply presidents, and I'm not out to trick you or be unfair about that. But, first of all, does that pattern as far as presidents of municipalities are concerned, this is 37 of the municipalities, but does that now tie in, with the best of your recollection, that in fact it was only a very tiny number of presidents of municipalities who were also deputies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I think you were suggesting that beyond presidents of municipalities, that there were a number of other people who held other positions in municipalities who were also deputies; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- but just moving for the moment, then, to the presidents of municipalities who were not deputies, which it's pretty clear was overwhelmingly most of them: You say, do you, that Mr. Krajisnik had influence over those people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a group or because he particularly knew specific individuals within that category?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Krajisnik wielded great authority and political power among the Serbian people in the earlier Joint Assembly and that those people who later became presidents of municipalities came to consult with Mr. Krajisnik as far as the parliamentary branch of municipal government was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mandic, can we be very clear: Do you know that? Do you know that presidents of municipalities who were not also deputies went to consult or did consult Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the basis or source of your own personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see them at Mr. Krajisnik's in the course of 1992. I even knew some of them personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You presumably didn't know very many of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost none of them, actually, personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't at any of these, if they were meetings, between the presidents of municipalities and Mr. Krajisnik, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't at any of the meetings. But I had personal knowledge that some presidents of municipalities came to consult with him. I believe it was mostly those from Sarajevo and the area there that went to see Mr. Krajisnik because it wasn't a great deal for them to come to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know yourself the content of their discussions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about going back to those presidents of municipalities who were deputies, and those deputies who were just deputies? Do you say that Mr. Krajisnik had influence over them beyond what would simply be expected from a respected and, by all accounts, energetic and efficient president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this a moment ago, and I will repeat it now: In this brief period of time, Mr. Krajisnik grew up to be a man who was held in highest esteem and who held most authority in the eyes of the people. Even from the perspective of the deputies, he was an excellent chairman of these sessions, and people would come to him, approach him to consult him, and I believe that he continued discharging his duties equally well afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was an excellent chairman, was he, in the -- well, the qualities of an excellent chairman, I suggest to you, he was an excellent chairman in the sense that he was efficient, businesslike, fair, and approached matters with an equable temperament?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in his public appearances, and there were appearances on television, weren't there? That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. All of us, myself included, expressed our positions in an emotional way when it came to these inter-ethnic problems. As for Mr. Krajisnik, he approached the topic in a quite different manner, with equanimity that he presented a position and his views when it came to the Serbian side, and the other sides that came to be at war together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, his public pronouncements were conspicuously free of aggressive language, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave some evidence about Mr. Karadzic's and Mr. Krajisnik's - they were bracketed together in a lot of the questioning - you gave some evidence about their ability, and of course we're specifically very interested in Mr. Krajisnik in this trial, their ability to influence or control entry into government posts. You remember talking about that in your evidence and in your earlier interviews with the OTP, do you -- sorry, with the Prosecution. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself were not a party to any significant discussions about government appointments at ministerial level, were you, leaving your own position aside?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, since I wasn't a member of the party, I didn't have access to these meetings. It was the political leadership, or rather, the top of the Serbian Democratic Party that decided on these matters and held consultations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were, so far as you could see, is this right, Mr. Mandic, there were, as there often are in politics, there were informal meetings, informal group discussions of those in leadership positions to discuss prospective appointments?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of the newly formed Serb Republic, and Republika Srpska, as it came to be known, it's right, isn't it, that a considerable number, a very high proportion of the government jobs were filled by people who had been engaged in broadly similar activities within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the split?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was especially true of the first government, because all the ministers except for Mr. Nikolic were of Serb ethnicity, including deputy ministers who used to form part of the joint government, were transferred into the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and assigned different functions there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first government, then, by the first government, you would carry that right through under Mr. Djeric, would you, right through to when he resigned and Mr. Lukic took over?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it follows, then, that, so far as those posts were concerned, where people broadly carried on with similar functions to the ones they'd had under the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there wasn't a great deal to argue about, there wasn't a great deal to debate, as far as appointments were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the Council of Ministers that we mentioned a moment ago. All the people who were in the Council of Ministers came from the joint government, and it was from the ranks of those staff that the first government was formed, Mr. Djeric's. Two members became members of the Presidency, president of the Assembly became the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People, and Mr. Djeric was a minister in the joint government of Jure Pelivan's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said in your evidence, and this was at page 79 of the transcript on Tuesday, the 23rd of November, you said that if there was -- if there had been a divergence of views between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, then usually it would be Mr. Karadzic's person who would be elected. And you said that was rare. Having identified it as rare, could you -- are you able now -- it's years later, but are you able to recall an example of a particular candidate or prospective government member over whom Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik disagreed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be on the safe side, let's take my case, for instance. I was supposed to be the head of the police, as the most senior police officer from the joint MUP. And at Mr. Karadzic's insistence, Mico Stanisic was appointed to that post, contrary to what Mr. Krajisnik had wanted. This is an example that I can take to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be -- it's almost a quarter to. If that were convenient to Your Honours, that would be a suitable point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is a convenient moment to you, Mr. Stewart, we'll have a break. We'll have a break until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Mandic into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I take the time. I asked myself why the laptop was not yet on Mr. Krajisnik's desk, where I signed already a few weeks ago. I do understand that the laptop is there, that it's just a matter of a signature for the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. The signature is not the hard bit, Your Honour. The agreement has raised questions in people's minds. We only had the agreement the last few days. It's obviously been some time in gestation. It's not a three-line document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'll then see what happens. But since I signed a couple of weeks ago, I wondered what happened, and I do understand that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- everyone's full attention at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That first of all the laptop is there and that the agreement has everyone's full attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it would to some extent, Your Honour, the problem has perhaps been that over the last few days it hasn't had everyone's full attention. But we'll speed it along as soon as we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's now concentrate again on the continuation of the cross-examination of Mr. Mandic. Mr. Mandic, I apologise for being involved in another matter when you entered the courtroom. Mr. Stewart will now resume his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you -- my microphone. Mr. Mandic, you were played a transcript of a telephone conversation between yourself and Mr. Lugonja. That is at page 80 of Thursday's transcript and page 8680 of the continuous transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked about Mr. Prstojevic. In the conversation, this is at page 81 of that transcript, Mr. Lugonja said, after the first fairly robust sentence, he said: "Tomo is pulling to his side because he's from the police. I believe that he's -- that he's mainly right." Then there's Prstojevic, the president of the party and of the Crisis Staff, and there's Kezunovic, the prime minister, you know, and you acknowledged yes. And then Mr. Lugonja said to me it seems this Kezunovic guy is right most of the time. Now, it looks, Mr. Mandic, and say whether this is right, that Mr. Lugonja is explaining to you who Mr. Prstojevic is and who Mr. Kezunovic is. So it certainly looks as if you don't yourself at this point when you're talking to Mr. Lugonja have any personal knowledge of the positions and personalities and issues that are occurring there in Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. He's really having to explain to you from scratch who the people are, what they're up to, what the issue is; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm trying to find on the Thursday transcript, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Did I say Thursday, Your Honour? My apologies if I -- I've done it again, I think, Your Honour. I've taken the wrong day of the week. Tuesday, the 23rd was what I -- I did say Thursday, and I didn't give the date. That's entirely my fault, Your Honour. It's Tuesday, the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The continuous transcript reference was probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, you were given an erroneous starting point for the first page of that sequential transcript. It's not 8600, it's 8544. The other pages are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had a system. The system broke down, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't explain it, we'll not understand. It's better. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The system was brilliant. The number was the wrong thing. Yes. I apologise for the wrong date. Tuesday, the 23rd of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic. The date issue. But so he was -- he was explaining from scratch to you. The -- and then when he said, and I don't know -- Mr. Mandic, if at some point you need to be refreshed by having this in front of you; in fact, that might be a good idea. It's Exhibit P413, so the witness, obviously, will need the B/C/S version. I'll try to find it as best I can for you, Mr. Mandic. There's a passage that begins, and it's at page 82 of the transcript, 6626. Mr. Lugonja says: "Well, it's impossible fucking hell Koljevic came last night. They closed themselves in there and won't let anyone in. A meeting, pal. What fucking kind of behaviour is that? That's just a bunch of fucking crooks." Do you see that passage, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lugonja makes it fairly easy to find, doesn't he. And then you say, Mr. Mandic: "Well, yeah. They're running to the boss. All right. I'll talk to Koljevic and up there to Karadzic." When you say "Well, yeah. They're running to the boss," who are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you understand, when Mr. Lugonja was saying: "They closed themselves in there and won't let anyone in," who it was who had closed themselves in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said it was Kezunovic, Tomo Kovac, and this Prstojevic person. It was the Crisis Staff, the leadership of the municipality of Ilidza at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it that Mr. Koljevic had been shut out? Is that what you understood? Or that he'd come along in response to a complaint about them closing themselves? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to me that they locked themselves in with Koljevic and didn't allow Petar Lugonja to attend that meeting. I was not let in on those events and the staffing, the appointments, but I had known Petar Lugonja for many years, and he was trying to tell me about some problems in Ilidza, and he was trying to get me, as deputy minister of MUP, or minister of justice, to get some people around Karadzic to listen to reason and to help solve these problems at Ilidza. It was rather a private line of communication then, unofficial line, because Pero and I had been friends for ten years before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it -- was this an issue that you were -- he was a friend of yours, but was it one that you were rather reluctant to get drawn into?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was part of the inner circle of the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party and the structures of power in Ilidza, and he didn't exactly find his place in the struggle for power that ensued after the war, and he was trying to present his view of the government in Ilidza through me, as his friend, while Prstojevic and his entourage were standing in his way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic. Apologies for interrupting. Ms. Cmeric suggests that the -- you -- in the end you received the question in the wrong form. It was your reluctance that I was asking about. I think you may have got it as Mr. Lugonja's reluctance, so I'll repeat it. Was this an issue that you, Mr. Mandic, were rather reluctant to get drawn into?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any official power to resolve this conflict in Ilidza, but I was trying to use my authority to help Petar Lugonja to get to the people at the top and tell them what the real situation was, like at Ilidza, because Kezunovic and to some extent Tomo Kovac were preventing him from doing that. And after that, I heard an intercept of a conversation between me and Tomo Kovac, which seems to be a continuation of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you were rather reluctant to get drawn into. Now you're explaining what happened. But the question was whether you were reluctant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the answer, please, Mr. Mandic? Well, you said "right," but I didn't know whether you were acknowledging the question or giving the answer. So can we be clear: Were you reluctant to be drawn into this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was. I was reluctant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, take up the issue with either or both of Mr. Koljevic and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so he having asked to have that problem resolved, if you don't remember -- you're not aware of Mr. Lugonja having had any direct contact himself over this issue with either Mr. Koljevic or Dr. Karadzic, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he actually managed to reach these two men, and very soon after this conversation he left Ilidza for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's at least quite possible that nobody took up this issue at all with Mr. Koljevic or Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know, then would you agree that it's possible?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- Mr. Prstojevic was a deputy in the Assembly. I don't think there's an issue about that. You were asked whether he had a relationship with Mr. Krajisnik, was he close to Mr. Krajisnik. And then you said: "I think --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to retract something I just put to you, Mr. Prstojevic [sic], because you were asked -- this is at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where Mr. Stewart said Mr. Prstojevic, he meant Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I meant Mr. Mandic, of course I did. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you were asked, and this was at page 84 of the transcript, so that's 8628: "Was Mr. Prstojevic a deputy in the Assembly?" And you said yes. In fact, I put it to you that he was not a deputy in the Assembly. So thinking about it now, I suppose question number one is: Do you accept you could have been wrong in asserting that he was a deputy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but I still saw him at Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were asked: "Did he --" on that same page: "Did he, Mr. Prstojevic, have a relationship with Mr. Krajisnik? Was he close to Mr. Krajisnik?" Your answer was: "I think that Mr. Krajisnik had major influence over Mr. Prstojevic as a deputy in the Assembly. Well, on the footing, and it's a checkable fact, Mr. Mandic, so let's proceed on the footing that Mr. Prstojevic was not a deputy in the Assembly, would you accept, then, that Mr. Krajisnik did not have major influence over Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did Mr. Krajisnik's major influence over Mr. Prstojevic come from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, Mr. Prstojevic would come to see the president of the Assembly for consultations, and it seems to me also that they knew each other and met frequently within the party, at party meetings. Mr. Krajisnik is from Rajlovac and Mr. Prstojevic is from Ilidza. I'm certain that Mr. Prstojevic respected Mr. Krajisnik, both as speaker of the Assembly and as one of the leaders and influential politicians within the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let's be clear about different things. I don't need or wish to challenge your assertion that Mr. Prstojevic respected Mr. Krajisnik. I don't have an issue about that. But I'm asking you about the source of what you -- or basis of what you describe as "major influence." Now, what are you able to tell the Trial Chamber from your own knowledge about the degree of influence that Mr. Krajisnik had over Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I really thought that he was a deputy in the Assembly, a president of a municipality, a man from Sarajevo who frequently went to Pale for consultations, I believed, in view of his frequent conversations with Mr. Krajisnik, that he bowed to his advice. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, would you agree: It seems to follow from the fact that you didn't even know that Mr. Prstojevic was not a deputy, that you can't have been that familiar with Mr. Prstojevic and his political connections? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was an inference I made from my personal observations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred -- this is at page 88 of the transcript. Same day. We haven't left that day. You referred to great animosity on the part of Mr. Djeric vis-a-vis Mr. Krajisnik, and that he thought - and "he" is obviously Mr. Djeric - he thought that, as prime minister, he should exercise a great deal more of power and that he should then act in accordance with government decisions. Now, Mr. Mandic, did you actually witness yourself in some way great animosity on the part of Mr. Djeric towards Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when do you say that started?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me it started immediately. When I say "immediately," I mean as soon as the war began, and when the first government and the first Serbian Assembly were established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did it -- how did it manifest itself that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I, as member of the cabinet, attended many cabinet sessions and I communicated with the prime minister. And in a way, he was very derisive about certain positions held by Mr. Krajisnik and certain decisions made by him. He viewed them as insufficiently good or insufficiently mature or, alternatively, as interfering with his own power or work, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give a specific example of something which provoked some hostility or disparagement or animosity towards Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall a specific example, but I think at the very outset, Mr. Djeric sided with Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic in their condemnation of and resistance towards Mr. Krajisnik, which was later felt through the institution of the government and the ministries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it personal or political, if you -- do you accept and understand the distinction that I'm putting? Apparently you do. So was it personal or political?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me it was of a personal nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever notice any corresponding hostility by Mr. Krajisnik toward Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was conflict, wasn't there, between Mr. Djeric, on the one hand, and you and Mr. Stanisic, on the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the -- well, I suppose I'd better start in this way. Was the -- I had said there was conflict between Mr. Djeric be, on the one hand, and you and Mr. Stanisic, on the other. You please tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Mandic, is it necessary to draw a distinction between you and Mr. Stanisic for these purposes, or can we proceed on the basis that in this area of conflict with Mr. Djeric, you and Mr. Stanisic basically stood as one?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say in my own name that I thought those professional professors to be irresponsible, I mean Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, and to some extent Mr. Djeric, who was a real professor, an academic person, and I expressed that at meetings, during my contacts with them, and my personal relations with them, which disrupted our relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, may I again ask you to listen carefully to the question. The question was whether you and Mr. Stanisic basically stood as one. And I didn't hear any answer to that question specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were not -- we did not stand as one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I should make it clear, Mr. Mandic, and with respect, Your Honour, that I qualified it with "for these purposes." I wasn't intending or attempting to elicit from you some general statement that you and Mr. Stanisic were always the same on every issue. In relation to conflict between Mr. Djeric, on the one hand, and you and Mr. Stanisic, I was just wishing to start by knowing whether we should draw a distinction between his conflict with you and his conflict with Mr. Stanisic, or whether, for the purposes of this particular issue, we can treat you and Mr. Stanisic as one.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, as minister of the interior of the MUP, was more accountable to the head of state and the command of the army, whereas I was reporting exclusively to the government, that is, Mr. Djeric. So our conflicts were not identical. We did not have these conflicts on identical grounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the conflict between Mr. Djeric and Mr. Stanisic, what was the source or basis of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basis of that conflict was that Mr. Stanisic, as minister of the MUP, was answerable mostly to the head of state and the commander of the army, that is, the chief of General Staff, and to a much lesser extent to the prime minister. For instance, Mr. Djeric did not agree that without his consent, the police should be able to mount an action or take any step, whereas Mr. Stanisic thought such consent unnecessary, and he only sought the agreement of the president of the Republic or the chief of the General Staff. I believe that is the essence of the conflict. It was basically a conflict between civilian authorities and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On his side, did you see whether Mr. Krajisnik supported or opposed Mr. Djeric in his position as prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really notice that Mr. Krajisnik took any specific position. I don't think he was involved, or he didn't want to be drawn in to that conflict. If you mean the relationship between Stanisic and Djeric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, and this is at the top of page 89 on the 23rd of November, which is 8643, you said that: "For a while, he" - that's Mr. Djeric - "didn't even want to communicate with Mr. Krajisnik." Was that expressed to you by Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't say that in so many words, but I could notice that he avoided speaking to or meeting with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know, do you, Mr. Mandic, from your own personal knowledge, whether in fact Mr. Djeric achieved a practice of non-communication with Mr. Krajisnik for any period?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked, on the same page, about the reasons why Mr. Djeric left his position as prime minister. The -- now, first of all, this is correct, isn't it, that there were 20 signatories produced, or 20 signatures produced within the Assembly to get rid of Mr. Djeric? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there -- do you remember: Was there a particular, specific issue, or was that a reflection of some fairly general dissatisfaction with Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a misunderstanding and differences on both sides, from the deputies, on the one hand, and Mr. Djeric, on the other. I think it was at the Zvornik Assembly session, held on the 16th of November, when Prime Minister Djeric, after several hours of discussion, submitted his resignation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' addition. Witness said irrevocable resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In your last answer, Mr. Mandic, did you include a reference to a dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you have in mind, Mr. Stewart? You mean in reference to the deputies or to Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain. What's happened is that the answer which I'm reading from the English transcript as from line 9: "I think there was a misunderstanding and differences on both sides." It's suggested to me that your answer was: "I think there was dissatisfaction and differences on both sides."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, well, in fact the 20 -- it was a petition of sorts and the 20 signatories who wished to get rid of Mr. Djeric, say -- they were, as you have already indicated to the Trial Chamber, they were successful, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Djeric who submitted his resignation, rather than having been removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he jumped, because he was about to be pushed, didn't he?
