utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave some evidence at page 92, 8636, you gave some evidence about Mr. Krajisnik and particular people who enjoyed his confidence, and you identified some of them. And what you said there was: "Well" -- you were asked to identify them, and you said: "Well, for the most part, they were deputies from the pre-war Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and presidents of municipalities who were appointed to those positions at the beginning of the war." And then the particular names you gave were Professor Vojislav Maksimovic, Petar Cancar, and Velibor Ostojic. And you continued: "And these people who were involved in parliamentary work before the war and at the beginning of the war, inter alia." Professor Maksimovic, what do you say from your observation, your knowledge, what was the basis of a particular relationship of confidence between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Maksimovic was head of the club of deputies of the SDS and was a deputy of the pre-war parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Krajisnik, of course, being the president of the pre-war Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, obviously knew Professor Maksimovic from that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Cancar, Petar Cancar?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Cancar was also a deputy in the pre-war Assembly and chairman of one of the councils of the pre-war Assembly. Later on, he became one of the key people in the parliament of the Serbian people, and for a while he was also a minister of justice, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Much later on, presumably, minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was much later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his key position in the Assembly, do you mean any sort of formal position or just that he was an active, respected member?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Petar Cancar was chairman of one of the councils in the pre-war Assembly. It was -- or rather, the chamber. It was the chamber of the peoples. I don't know which of the two parliament chambers, but he must have been there for the speaker of one of the chambers of the pre-war Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Velibor Ostojic, the basis of -- of his relationship of confidence, as you suggested, with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recalled Mr. Ostojic at that moment because he was the -- one of those three people from Foca who was the minister of information in the pre-war government and he was minister of information later on as well. I believe it was in the first government. He was later on to become a deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, perhaps you could tell the Trial Chamber this. Well, let me first put this to you: Mr. Krajisnik you have described as being a respected, efficient, fair president of the Assembly, and he had been the same, had he, in terms of efficiency, energy, fairness, equable temperament, he'd been the same, had he, in his position as the president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly; is that right? He'd shown the same qualities, had he, and the same abilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you agree: It would have been astounding if, over a period, he hadn't developed relationships of confidence with at least a significant number of members of the Assembly over which he presided? Do you agree? He'd be a hopeless president, wouldn't he, if he didn't manage to achieve at least that much?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking at the time about three persons in whom Mr. Krajisnik in the beginning of the war placed most trust, who were closest to him in terms of politics, and he went along well with them. They were people of Mr. Krajisnik's confidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- perhaps we can clear something up here, then. So when you were asked to identify people who enjoyed Mr. Krajisnik's confidence, those three gentlemen - Mr. Maksimovic, Mr. Cancar, and Mr. Ostojic - you put those as three gentlemen who enjoyed particular clear and strong confidence of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among others, yes. In that particular moment, I thought of those three people. I could have mentioned some others too. I mentioned them because Cancar and Mr. Maksimovic were deputies, whereas Mr. Ostojic was a member of the pre-war government. And that's why I thought of them when Mr. Prosecutor asked of me to mention some names. That's when I recalled these three men, who were certainly very close associates of Mr. Krajisnik's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Mandic, would you be able -- then you said you could mention other names. Would you be able to give names of other people who enjoyed Mr. Krajisnik's special confidence, rather than -- if you see the distinction I'm suggesting, as opposed to members of the Assembly with whom it was natural that a president might establish a decent working relationship, so people with whom he enjoyed some clear, special degree of confidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had very special relations with members of his cabinet, with myself, for instance, he had very good relations on a very fair footing, and he placed a lot of confidence in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we suggest that what came across in the English interpretation as "cabinet" would be better translated as "office."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- Yes. Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Stewart, well, you made a mistake. I do the same. I apologise. I'd rather not have a new translation put in place for what you considered a wrong one, but verify with the witness, say: When you said that he had a special relation with members of, what did you say. Then the interpreters will have an opportunity. Otherwise it is suggested to the witness what you at least expect would be the proper translation, and I think we should keep that -- I try to draw the attention of the Defence to this before, but it might have been Ms. Loukas. So we seek with the witness to repeat what he said, and if there then is a remaining issue, the interpreters will be aware that there might be a translation issue and we'll try to sort it out in that way preferably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I take the point, Your Honours, indeed. Well, I -- it doesn't work so well in this particular case, but I apologise for that. But I wonder, Your Honour, if therefore we might test and run through this one as best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not think that it's a very -- so specific that we should repeat it, but just for the future. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps I might just put it, because I believe in this case it is not all that contentious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you described, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Krajisnik as having very special relations, you meant he had very special relations with people of his parliamentary office?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the people who cooperated with him, worked with him, Milos Savic, Nenad Radovic, people who were his immediate associates. I'm talking about his office, his associates who were with him since the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a degree of rivalry between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, but on that same page, page 92, you said -- you were asked: "Later, after, beyond 1992, did some rivalry -- did any rivalry between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik begin to develop -- well, begin to develop or appear to develop?" And you answered: "My personal opinion is that after a few years of the war, a few years into the war, there was a kind of rivalry that sprang up in terms of the exercise of power." Mr. Mandic, a few years is -- well, it's a few years. When you say that a kind of rivalry sprang up, casting your mind back as best you can, when do you say that this rivalry first emerged, as you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rivalry was, so it seems, created by the people in the government and in the president's office. It seems to have originated from the entourage, not, having, several years into the war, but rather after a few months of the war, that is, speaking of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik's entourage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, I have to ask you, therefore, why you've specifically told the Trial Chamber earlier that it was after a few years of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been a slip of the tongue, because the war lasted some three years or so. I mostly referred to 1991 and 1992, so there must have been an error.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, I'm inviting you to think carefully, because there's a double slip of the tongue because your answer was: "My personal opinion is that after a few years of the war, a few years into the war, there was a kind of rivalry." So when do you now say -- let's be as specific as we can, since there's a change here - when do you now say that this rivalry first began to appear?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, after the first year of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you start the war, in your mind, when?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this rivalry began to emerge, did it, in -- sometime in the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Or in late 1992. But somewhere around a year into the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you noticed this yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I myself, but some people observed this, and we discussed this matter quite frequently, the relationship between the president of the Assembly and the president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in Belgrade by that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was some of this on the level of political gossip?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what in these discussions, as they clearly were, then, what -- was something generally identified as the root cause of this rivalry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that the roots lay in the problems related to the staffing, at all levels of government in Republika Srpska, and in the relations between Republika Srpska and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at each of those, then. The problems related to staffing in Republika Srpska. So you're saying from these discussions, it appeared to you that there was some pronounced difference of view, was there, between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you summarise or encapsulate that difference of view in some way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my conversations with Mr. Krajisnik, I often mentioned this, also when talking to others, that whenever there would be some key persons appointed into the government or into public companies or other functions, Mr. Krajisnik would, under the influence of -- Mr. Krajisnik, would be dissatisfied with that appointment. Mr. Karadzic would be backed by Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic whenever it came to the appointments into public companies, some people with qualifications, or into ministerial positions in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the other limb, the other root, if you like, relations between Republika Srpska and Serbia: Again, can you summarise or encapsulate that difference of view in some way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic relied far more on the policies of Mr. Milosevic, whereas Mr. Krajisnik was in favour of an autonomous policy to be pursued by Republika Srpska, both vis-a-vis the Federation, that is, the other warring party, and in terms of its foreign policy. I believe that the differences of opinion in that area were far greater. In my personal opinion, Dr. Karadzic was greatly influenced by Mr. Milosevic, and that was not the case with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your own -- you've described yourself as being close to Mr. Krajisnik. Now, the evidence you have given today and earlier I think as well in this trial, you've told the Trial Chamber you actually didn't know Mr. Krajisnik early in 1991, so that such closeness as you developed was over the next year. Did that -- well, first of all, how -- what would you say was the point at which your political relationship to Mr. Krajisnik was at its closest?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talked of the political views, but rather about the relationship between the two persons. When those critical months of the beginning of the war came, I frequently consulted with Mr. Krajisnik, who was at least to me, in my opinion, the most serious politician in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, unlike Mr. Nikola Koljevic and Ms. Biljana Plavsic, who, for instance, would freeze her position in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and then go on some private errands visiting monasteries, churches, and so on. Unlike her, Mr. Krajisnik tried to help me in any way he could in the different relations existing within the pre-war MUP and in developing the new MUP, or rather, the new justice system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So leaving aside any label of personal or political, but taking your own description of your relations with Mr. Krajisnik, as you've just given it, when do you say was the point at which your relationship to Mr. Krajisnik reached its closest?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was the end of 1991, and it was also throughout the war, but also in the aftermath of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you did develop quite a warm personal relationship with Mr. Krajisnik, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not close in terms of being friends or on visiting terms. It was a relationship of respect, particularly vis-a-vis Mr. Krajisnik. I knew that he was going to do anything possible, if it was within his power, to solve any matters that I approached him with, and that was true for any walks of life, from private matters to state matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave some evidence and you were asked questions -- this is on Wednesday, the 24th of November. This is at page 26, which is going to be 8663 of the continuous transcript. You were asked about a way in which financial support had been given in relation to Sokolac when apparently officially the funding for the police station in Sokolac had been suspended. You recall that evidence? I'll remind you of it if you want, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you remember, or --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can refresh my memory, yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I will, then. You were --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please remind me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give you the same refresher that Mr. Tieger gave you, in fact, from your interview. You said: "At the time I had a special cash register as the head of one of the ministry departments and since Zoran Cvijetic, God rest his soul, was the head of police in Sokolac, who jumped before all of us and didn't exactly behave by the agreed policy. He fired all employees of Muslim nationality before everybody else did, and as a result, the police station in Sokolac was suspended. Of course, people had to receive their salaries, to buy fuel and everything else, because they didn't have means to live and work. In the agreement with Mico Stanisic, who -- he was already Serbian minister of Serbian MUP, but with the knowledge of Radovan Karadzic, I transferred the means from that cash register to Sokolac. That was to cover the salaries, the fuel, and all that. That was very risky move which I hid in the paperwork and decisions, saying that some of it went to Banja Luka, some of it to Medici, and that was the way we kept the station going for two months." And then you did in your evidence go on to say that it wasn't quite -- it wasn't exactly like that. But, Mr. Mandic, I'm not -- at the moment, I'm not intent on exploring the differences between your interview and your evidence and getting into the details of that. My question is a very simple one. Mr. Krajisnik wasn't involved in any of this, was he, and didn't have any knowledge about any of this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about Exhibit 420, which I wonder if you can be given. That is a document which you do acknowledge signing, don't you, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said specifically, and this is at page 41, 8678, that you were instructed by the newly appointed minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, to send this kind of telegram, and that's what I did."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have given evidence that, as far as you were concerned, this was in accordance with decisions which had already been taken on behalf of the Serbian people. But Mr. Krajisnik himself had no individual part in the preparation and dissemination of this particular document, did he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. At that moment, Mr. Krajisnik was in Lisbon, together with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and I believe Mate Boban, where they signed the so-called Cutileiro Plan. This plan verified the creation of armies and police forces based on ethnicity, and Mr. Stanisic informed me about this. He said that in keeping with the decisions of the Assembly and the enactments stated in the dispatch, I was supposed to circulate this across the territory to all police stations and all autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I suppose my first point, Mr. Mandic, it may seem like a digression: You'd agree that there has now come into your head very specifically a recollection that Mr. Krajisnik was involved in international negotiations and was at times abroad on those negotiations? That's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you say Mr. Stanisic -- what information did Mr. Stanisic give you that you needed, in other words, that you didn't already have?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew about the decisions of the Assembly of the Serbian People and I knew about the enactment of this constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the enactment of the law on Internal Affairs, which I stated, enumerated in this dispatch. He only informed me that the Cutileiro Plan was initialled in Lisbon and that I was to circulate this dispatch to all field offices in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- this is back at page 11, which is 8648 - you referred to decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the establishment of a Serbian MUP. When do you say that decision had been reached?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch says at a session held on the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was promulgating the constitution of the Serbian Republic. That's what it records. That's what you're talking about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This session also adopted the law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's the law on Internal Affairs which is applicable here; that's what you're talking about, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was enacted by the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at page 11, the page we just referred to, you were talking about Mr. Radovic speaking after Mr. Stanisic at the meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, and you said: "Mr. Radovic speaking after Mr. Stanisic, discussed the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the establishment of a Serbian MUP." You clearly couldn't have been talking about a decision of the 27th of March, because that hadn't arrived yet, so you were talking about some other decision prior to the 11th of February, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please clarify that, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The passage that I cited to you a few minutes ago, where you had talked about discussion of the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the establishment of a Serbian MUP, came in a question. The question, page 11, the reference I've already given, Mr. Radovic, speaking after Mr. Stanisic, and you were talking about the meeting of the 11th of February, 1992. It was put to you by Mr. Tieger: "Mr. Radovic, speaking after Mr. Stanisic, discussed the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the establishment of a Serbian MUP?" And you said: "Correct. Before this meeting, the Assembly of the Serb People in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina reached a decision on the establishment of a Serb MUP, and I think that on that occasion, a law was passed, a law on the MUP." So your recollection was that the decision and the law on the MUP had arisen before the 11th of February. That was your recollection, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have been mistaken about the dates. I would be grateful if you could give me the transcript of the session in Banja Luka, and then maybe I would be able to explain. Is it the case that a decision was made to do something, or the law was enacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to remember exactly when we have the break. I think this is about the time when we normal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is approximately the time when we usually have the break. The witness would like to have a look at the transcript. I don't know whether I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's what I had in mind, Your Honour. It seemed more convenient to have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To find that during the break, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until five minutes to 6.00. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the registrar, that's Exhibit 415, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you asked to have an opportunity, which it's fair that you should have, to refresh your recollection in relation to the meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, 1992, and that is Exhibit 415. The very first thing that I'm going to ask you to do, Mr. Mandic, if I may, and following something His Honour Judge Orie said before the break, is to invite you to read the second paragraph, which appears under the heading of the name of Mr. Stanisic. Do you see that? Just fairly shortly down the first page, there's a reference to Mr. Stanisic and then there's a paragraph which starts in English: "The Ministerial Council's position ..." And I'm going to invite you just to read the first sentence of the next -- well, it's all one sentence, actually -- to read the next paragraph, the one that begins: "The MUP ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior, MUP, of the SRBH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you could continue, please. Sorry. I beg your pardon, Mr. Mandic. If you'll read it out loud. I'm so sorry. If you could read the whole of that paragraph out loud, until I invite you to stop.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The MUP of the SRBH is held by the Muslims rather than by the Serbs, contrary to what the general public is being led to believe, because the SDA has about 1.000 people in reserve forces of the police in the Stari Grad police station, out of whom only 30 or so are Serbs, who almost do not even have uniforms, unlike the others, who are armed with the most modern weapons."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You can --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Work should be done --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can stop, Mr. Mandic. We've got past the critical point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I apologise. I'm trying to avoid troubling you to also be a linguistic expert, though I'm sure you can be in appropriate circumstances. But the first few words which appear in the Serbian as "MUP SRBIH," "dijele muslimani," perhaps you could just tell the Trial Chamber what's the sense of "dijele"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of days ago, when answering the questions of the Prosecution, I said that when nationalist parties came into power, they demanded that the Ministry of the Interior should have the same structure as the national structure of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian. If, for instance, there was a 35 per cent Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there should be 35 per cent of Muslim staff on the police. At that moment, most of the policemen were Serbs, and the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, that is, the government, demanded that police stations be reinforced from the ethnic community of Muslims, parallel with dismissing Serb policemen, in order to reflect the ratio of the ethnic communities within the country. I hope I have managed to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask through Your Honour: The question -- what's arisen is a question as to the appropriateness of the translation that we're reading in 415, in the first line or two of that paragraph. I'm afraid I don't know, Your Honour, whether the interpreters' booth are doing a fresh translation now or whether they're reading from that. Because that may indicate the difficulty. It's being suggested to me that the translation we're seeing in the document is not correct, but we're getting the same translation again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apology. We did read this word out rather than interpreting it, which was a mistake, and the word is actually "is being divided by the Muslims, not held by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The apology is due from me not making it absolutely clear what I was inviting the interpreters to do and the purpose of the exercise. So thank you very much, interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then just ask whether the translation would be that the -- I'll just try to understand it. That the MUP of the socialist Republic BiH is divided rather by the Muslims than by the Serbs. Is that a correct understanding of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Being divided, I think what was suggested, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Being divided by the Muslims rather than by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. That took a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have spent moments less efficiently. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we've got that cleared up, Mr. Mandic. And then you were there, of course, at this meeting, and your -- well, he was your boss, wasn't he, really, Mr. Stanisic, was saying that -- the paragraph after that: "Work should be done on the organisation of a Serbian MUP, starting with municipal and regional branches." Now, at that point, Mr. Mandic, it sounds - say whether this is wrong - it sounds as if this is being put forward by Mr. Stanisic as a proposal that there should be a separate Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Stanisic was conveying here the position of the Ministerial Council stated in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Stewart proceeds, a small correction. I don't think the evidence reflects that Mr. Stanisic was Mr. Mandic's boss at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I beg your pardon. I think that is right, actually. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I jumped ahead as far as that goes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- when we look at Mr. Radovic's remark, it's quite a short intervention by Mr. Radovic below that, which you had referred to, he informed those present that the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a decision on the establishment of Serbian MUP and he presented the text and the content thereof to the attendees. We're not a hundred per cent sure about the Serbian there, Mr. Mandic, but is it your recollection that Mr. Radovic referred to such a matter or that he actually read or put before the meeting some actual text of a document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we should first distinguish between these enactments. Nenad Radovic informed those present that the Assembly passed only a decision, not the law, on the establishment of the Serbian MUP. So in that month, the Assembly took the decision to establish the Serbian MUP. And he was informing the Serbs present about the text of that decision. Not the law. The law was passed on the 27th March 1992. At this particular moment, there was only a decision to establish the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if the witness might, therefore, have -- it's a document already in evidence. It was in Mr. Treanor's exhibits. It's P65. It's folder 9A, tab 103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, and the same is true, of course, for the Prosecution. If you foresee that you would need one of the many, many documents of Mr. Treanor, could you perhaps give already a message to the registrar so that she can start finding them in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies, Your Honour. I didn't foresee until about five minutes ago, but I still could have done it during those five minutes. So we'll certainly try and remember to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is Law on Internal Affairs, published in the Official Gazette on the 23rd of March, 1992, and it is setting out Law on Internal Affairs enacted by the National Assembly, it's described as, but the Assembly of Republika Srpska, at its session of the 28th of February, 1992. Is this -- at least you have the advantage of being a lawyer, Mr. Mandic, but if you could just look at it sufficiently to confirm that that's the document that you had in mind by your reference to the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the -- is the explanation this: If we're looking -- I don't know whether we are literally looking, but if we're considering the document which you sent out, dated the 31st of March, 1992, the 420 that we'd referred to before, that's your signed document on the instructions of Mr. Stanisic relating to the setting up of the Serbian MUP, in that document, you began by saying: "At its meeting held on 27th of March, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina ... promulgated the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then lower down, you talk about -- you say: "In that respect, it passed a Law on Internal Affairs, which shall be uniformly applied on the territory of the Republic of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina as of 1st of April, 1992, and appointed Mico Stanisic until now an advisor in the BH MUP, as minister." Is the explanation that the constitution was promulgated on the 27th of March, 1992, but the Law on Internal Affairs was earlier. It's this document. This was passed at the session on the 28th of February? That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the Law on Internal Affairs could be passed before the passing of the constitution as the supreme law. Then the constitution must have been passed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It just doesn't seem all that likely, Mr. Mandic, with the greatest respect. This apparently quite significant document that's reciting the -- I'm paying you a compliment here, in effect, Mr. Mandic, that's reciting these documents. You would have taken care to make sure that the basic recitals were correct, wouldn't you, you and your colleagues in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I provided the information that I had in this dispatch, because I did not attend the Assembly sessions where the constitution and the Law on Internal Affairs were passed. But obviously, the Law on Internal Affairs was not passed before the 11th of February, 1992, but only a decision to establish the Serbian MUP, at an extended Ministerial Council meeting, where Mr. Stanisic was present as a member of the council, and there was the Assembly decision, and only 16 days later was the Law on Internal Affairs actually passed by the Assembly. Therefore, this particular document, my dispatch, and this meeting in Banja Luka explain the course in which the events took place in terms of the Assembly, the Ministerial Council, and the Serb members of the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us then, Mr. Mandic. In the document that you sent out dated the 31st of March, 1992, you said, it's three paragraphs down in that document: "On the day this law comes into force," that's the Law on Internal Affairs, because there's no other law you're referring to, "the security services centre and public security stations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are abolished and cease to function, and their authority, i.e., tasks and duties within the competence of organs of Internal Affairs are taken over by the above-mentioned organisational units of MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Can you help us, Mr. Mandic? You've got the document in the original Serbian there. Where do we find that specific provision? It's quite a long document, including some stuff about school uniforms, so I -- can you assist the Trial Chamber, and me, incidentally, to identify where in this document, Law on Internal Affairs, we find the provisions relating to the ceasing of functioning of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP and the duties being taken over by the MUP of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I don't know if it's an important aspect of the cross-examination that the witness actually search for it or if it would be helpful if I identify a likely --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no objection whatever to Mr. Tieger speeding us to the right point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you refer to 126, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We see -- thank you for that. 126, that's what you're referring to in your document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the 127 is consequential on that, is it, as far as -- well, it's more general, but it's consequential as far as MUP employees are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This was regulated by the Law on Internal Affairs, as I had mentioned in my dispatch. It seems to me that I also mentioned the Sarajevo Agreement. This was an agreement on the Cutileiro Plan that was verified in Lisbon on the 30th of March, a day before the dispatch was sent out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the particular point you're making in relation to the Sarajevo Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Sarajevo Agreement hinges on this. The agreement on the cantonisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina along the ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't the position this: That among other things, the Sarajevo Agreement did contemplate arrangements which would include a separate Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your recollection -- and we -- most of this is checkable as far as documents are concerned, Mr. Mandic, but in your recollection there was a decision of the Assembly before the meeting on the 11th of February. There was the meeting of the 11th of February in Banja Luka, at which you were present. There was subsequently, as we see, 28th of February Assembly session at which the Law on Internal Affairs was passed containing this provision, essentially consistent with an element of the Sarajevo agreement, Cutileiro Plan, and then on the 31st of March, on the instructions of Mr. Stanisic, you issue a document which faithfully implements and reflects the Law on Internal Affairs which has been passed. Is that a correct sequence of events, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Law on Internal Affairs, as one would expect under the system in operation, it's signed by Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because that's what he is and that's the procedure which has to be adopted in relation to any law passed by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the Assembly signed all the documents promulgated by the president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so Mr. Krajisnik's part in this, he was the president of an Assembly which was supportive, in the sense that it actually positively approved and passed, supportive of a decision and eventually of a law that was consistent with that element in the Sarajevo Agreement, which you then signed in that way, but that is the limit of what you know about Mr. Krajisnik's involvement in this particular matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we simply invite you to do this, if we leave aside - we can argue about that, Mr. Krajisnik's position as president of the Assembly - every deputy of the Assembly who voted in favour of this proposal was giving the same individual support to the decision of the Assembly in the context as I've just outlined it to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence on Wednesday, the 24th of November, and this is at page 57 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'm giving up giving the other reference to the continuous transcript, because for technical rather than arithmetical reasons, it just doesn't work, so it doesn't help anybody. So I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I'm sticking with page 57, and, well, Mr. Tieger will have to do his best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about an interview, and this was an interview Exhibit number P424, though I don't think I need trouble you specifically with the exhibit for a moment, Mr. Mandic, unless we get stuck in some way. But you said -- included in that interview, it was actually the fifth question, so it's referred to page 57 as the transcript. You said: "As a man, I am very devoted to both Slobodan Milosevic and to Radovan Karadzic. With Karadzic and Krajisnik, I began the war in Sarajevo, and now, when I am sitting here and watching what happened, I find justification for the Serbian leadership of Yugoslavia." As a matter of fact, Mr. Mandic, I objected to that question, but never mind. That's the passage in the interview: "I began the war -- with Karadzic and Krajisnik, I began the war in Sarajevo." Now, that's a very large claim or admission, depending how one characterises it, Mr. Mandic. You were asked some questions about this. But with or without anybody else, is that really literally your position that you began the war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, first of all, I do not recall this interview. And only a part of it was shown to me. Now, whether these are sensationalist newspapers or merely views of these journalists there, I don't know, but I don't believe I placed myself among the political establishment of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think perhaps it is fair. It's a pretty sensitive area, Your Honours. I think it's fair, Mr. Mandic, that you should have that exhibit, 424.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It gives me, meanwhile, an opportunity, Mr. Tieger, to understand the previous document, which is the Treanor document, and a lot of questions. I noticed that in the English translation, we do neither find the date of the 28th of February, nor do we have a date of publication the 23rd of March. So in order to understand the testimony, I would at least have some additional information to the translation. Because the whole sequence in time is -- you can't follow that if you only have the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, we think what happened was that we were later supplied, very helpfully, by the Prosecution with a new or corrected or new, improved translation, which does have that information on it, and I was working from that. So that may be the explanation, in which case, clearly, one way or the other, we ought to ensure that that new, improved version finds its way to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course in the original you can more or less decipher the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's what happened, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've got a better, more informative version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please pay some attention to that, Mr. Tieger. Then if there is this better version, if we could see it and see whether it could be replaced, then, by the new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've got it, Your Honour, so there's no physical problem about that. We've actually got it in our hands here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you may proceed meanwhile. Because my ears and my eyes are two different functioning movements. Yes. That's exactly what gives the better information, the difference between the original in the Treanor binder and this version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll sort it out for Your Honours, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Prosecution would agree that this translation is replaced by this version, which is a version with all the headings, as we find them in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Certainly, Your Honour. And I'm pleased the Court brought that to our attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'll provide a copy and then Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can happily leave that with the Prosecution for the moment if it's easier for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure we had the correct ERN number so make sure there was no further complication. We can now return it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber expects a copy to be provided to Madam Registrar which could then replace it in the Treanor binder. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you've now got, I think -- you've seen it briefly before, but you've now got, I hope, a copy of an interview which apparently was published in something called Ekstra magazine. You have that? And the passage previously referred to and is being again now, is under the heading "How did you personally take the political conflict and severance of relations --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the second page left-hand column, I'm told, Mr. Mandic, and it says "How did you personally take the political conflict and severance of relations between Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?" And then it goes: "As a man, I'm very devoted ..." and so on. So you might want to just take a moment to refresh your memory and to, well, read that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's some years later, but I'll ask you the first question, Mr. Mandic. Do you actually have any recollection of giving such an interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This paper was, I think, from Bijeljina, this Ekstra magazine. I don't think it exists any longer. This was a weekly, what we would call yellow press. Here in the beginning, as I can see, it says: "Momcilo Mandic, a long-time and prominent member of the SDS," which isn't true, and probably there's other stuff that isn't true as well. I saw this for the first time when Mr. Tieger showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mandic, are you -- I just want to be clear. Are you suggesting that the journalist, the editors, might erroneously have included a passage referring to your assertion that you began the war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I was as ambitious as that at that time, either -- to define myself as the man who had started the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know how at all would I have been able to do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we take it, Mr. Mandic: We can exclude, as far as you're concerned, can we, the at least logically prior possibility that this article is a total fabrication and that no such interview with you took place and it's a complete invention? You wouldn't suggest such a startling position, would you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, Mr. Stewart, when I say that I don't remember this article and that I saw it for the first time when Mr. Tieger showed it to me. Evidently, this text dates from the time when I was head of the bureau in Belgrade, and this paper is from Bosnia, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to be clear whether you're suggesting that it is a possibility that the whole thing is a complete fabrication or whether we're at least starting from the position that you're acknowledging that some such interview took place, which is broadly reflected in this newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I don't remember this interview. I don't remember ever giving one, this one. There are some illogical assertions here that make no sense about my relationship with Karadzic and Milosevic that seems to exaggerate our intimacy. Then the fact that I was a prominent member of the Serbian Democratic Party. I have evidently never been a member of the SDS. And there are some other illogical matters here, and I really do not remember anything related to this article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a statement such as that, in whatever circumstances, at whatever time, is a statement such as that, that "I began the war in Sarajevo" one that you could and would ever have made?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it therefore --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would seem like really improper boasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid -- just for the moment, I -- it may have come up in the course of the evidence or subsequent discussion as to what the date of this article was. It was -- at the time it initially came up, it was going to be checked, but I'm afraid I now can't remember whether we were then subsequently informed of the date. I'm just wondering -- help. I'm wondering whether anybody else remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the information given to us was by the context, it was situated during the period when Mr. Mandic was in Belgrade. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect, I certainly agree with that. It didn't narrow it down terribly far, was I think the point. At the foot of page 49, Your Honour said: "Mr. Tieger, you're invited to give further details as soon as possible on the -- I'm invited to slow down: "Mr. Tieger, you're invited to give further details as soon as possible on the date of publication of the Ekstra magazine." And Mr. Tieger said: "I will advise the Court at the earliest opportunity." I apologise, Your Honour, if somewhere later in the transcript that opportunity was later taken and I've just overlooked it or -- I don't remember where it was. Well, my cry for help is going unheeded. I don't seem to be alone here in not knowing when it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic -- well, I know it's not really fair to ask you, Mr. Mandic, because you've said already you have no recollection whatever of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you provide any assistance, any further assistance? What I -- what my attention is drawn to is that at least reference is made to something that happened in September 1993, which suggests that this is after September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can only -- I can't provide additional guidance other than the type that the Court is engaged in now, that is, a contextual analysis of the document itself. As I understand it, when this document was obtained, it was copied in a manner that did not provide the date. I mean, I'm not in a position to actually determine the date specifically from a portion of the document in our possession. So the contextual analysis that we engaged in before and that the Court was conducting a moment ago is -- we can participate in that as well, but no further guidance is available, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's not a very narrow dating, but I note that on the last page of the English, a paragraph beginning: "As for September 1993 ..." And it begins -- sorry - it ends, I beg your pardon, the last sentence: "The September operation was organised for entirely different matters of which it will perhaps be possible to mention in five or ten years, perhaps when the war ends."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the same as on the bottom of page 4, where the article says something about the participants in the September 1993 operation. So that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it gives us a start and a finish, Your Honour. It's no earlier than September 1993, but it's no later than, well, the end of 1995, when we suppose that the war is taken to have ended. So it's two years, is the frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mandic, I suggest we can take it from your answers and confirm that -- I asked you whatever time, so during that period from after September 1993, while apparently the war was still continuing, according to the text and context, your evidence is that you could and would have never made any such statement that you started the war in Sarajevo. That's your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it follows, perhaps, as a piece of elementary logic, that if you would never have made any such statement that you began the war in Sarajevo, you therefore could and would not have made any statement that you began the war in Sarajevo with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, both of them, or anybody else in the world?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my evidence given so far to the Prosecution and to yourself, Mr. Stewart, it transpires that everything that happened in early 1992 doesn't fit in with any allusion that I started the war with Karadzic, Krajisnik, or whoever. This decision to establish the Serbian MUP was preceded by a number of incidents and skirmishes, and there was a series of events that followed from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without, if necessary, going into those, are you, by that comment, are you saying, Mr. Mandic, that the-- that the decision, from everything that you could see and knew at the time, that the decision to establish a separate Serbian MUP was a justified, reasonable decision to take and implement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows from that meeting in Banja Luka, where individual officials, Serbs, presented the problems encountered in the operation of the mixed MUP and that the growing numbers of Muslim policemen in the reserve forces of the MUP, and they were trying to point out these problems to Minister Alija Delimustafic. As for this meeting in Banja Luka, it was attended by highly qualified professionals, policemen who had been in the service for 10, 15 years, all of them graduates of a police academy when it was still a joint academy. And they were policemen before everything else. They expressed what they felt and thought. I'm speaking now about the meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, therefore, when you referred to -- you said "the decision to establish the Serbian MUP was preceded by a number of incidents and skirmishes," can we be clear which decision in that sequence of decisions and resolutions and laws and so on, which decision are you referring to then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People to establish a Serbian Ministry of the Interior. This decision was presented by Nenad Radovic, who read out the text of the decision. He was then assistant minister for appointments in the MUP. And Mr. Stanisic conveyed at the same meeting the conclusions of the Ministerial Council in its extended composition concerning the MUP, including the conclusion that a Serbian MUP should be established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the incidents and skirmishes that you referred to, because you said "this decision to establish the Serbian MUP was preceded by a number of incidents and skirmishes." So those incidents and skirmishes happened, well, certainly sometime before the 11th of February. They were in late 1991 and early 1992, were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you give an illustration of a skirmish that you have in mind as part of the background?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in February that we had a great problem committing a special unit of the MUP which went to ethnically pure areas populated by Serbs. They rounded up people and took them into custody, inspecting them for possession of weapons, et cetera. Those were incidents, and we had meetings in Krtelj with the leadership of the special unit, and at one point we reached an agreement that it may not be activated without the approval of three leaders of different ethnicities. I remember incidents in Bileca, in Foca, in the settlement of Pofalici in Sarajevo, in Stari Grad, and so on. Another great problem which I mentioned two or three times was the lack of control of enrolment in the police force. People were admitted without being vetted, and sometimes even criminals were engaged as policemen. Because the priority was to establish an ethnic composition of the police force which would reflect the exact ethnic composition of the country, which was impossible as an objective. I have to remind you: At the beginning, when the national parties only came into power, there were 10.000 employees in the Ministry of the Interior. I'm speaking only about the uniformed staff. Over 7.000 of them were Serbs. A little over 2.000 were Muslims, and very few were Croats. And that was a problem that the parties immediately emphasised as a problem and wanted an immediate change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, there's just part of this answer, I'd like to seek a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just don't understand it. Mr. Mandic, you said that there was a "great problem committing a special unit of the MUP which went to ethnically pure areas populated by Serbs." And then you say: "They rounded up people." Who are "they"? Is this the special unit of the MUP? Did the special unit of the MUP round up people and take them into custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The special unit was a unit for special purposes. Only upon the orders of the minister were they able to intervene on certain security missions and law enforcements missions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're explaining, but I'm just trying to understand what you said before. You said: "I think it was in February that we had a great problem committing a special unit of the MUP which went to ethnically pure areas populated by Serbs." And then you said: "They rounded up people and took them into custody, inspecting them for possession of weapons, et cetera." Who did you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The special unit, composed of policemen of all ethnicities - it was a mixed special unit - went to ethnically pure Serb settlements, searched houses, looking for weapons and arrested people. And that was a political problem vis-a-vis the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just asking who you meant by "they" and now I do understand by your answer that by "they," you meant the special unit of the MUP that went there. Now, you gave a few examples: "We reached an agreement that it may not be activated without the approval of three leaders of the different ethnicities. I remember incidents in Bileca, in Foca, in the settlement of Pofalici in Sarajevo, in Stari Grad, and so on." Earlier you referred to the special unit being committed to purely Serb areas. I do understand that this is not about sending them to purely Serb areas any more, or is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the examples you gave were mixed areas, or at least non-purely Serb areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I gave the example of Pofalici, Bileca, Foca, Stari Grad. They were purely Serb neighbourhoods and areas. Later, when political problems arose at the level of the Assembly among MPs, between parties, and within the Ministry of the Interior, we appointed three leaders of the special unit, or special units, each representing one of the ethnic groups, to decide together on any engagement, any missions of the special unit, to avoid future problems of the same kind that we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now at least I -- I was just trying to understand you. You say all the areas you mentioned, including Stari Grad and Pofalici, were purely Serb areas. Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. Well, we are close to 7.00 anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I mention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric suggests that the question that Your Honour asked, it's at line 20 to 22 of page 80, when Your Honour said: "I do understand this is not about sending them to purely Serb areas any more, or is it?" Ms. Cmeric suggests that it may be that the negative got dropped from the translation, which would explain an awful lot of what comes afterwards, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least now it's clear that the witness says that the four examples he gave were examples of where he's speaking about an intervention in purely Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and that seems to fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it's 7.00. We adjourn for the day. I have one procedural issue to deal with for a moment, but I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give, and we'd like to see you back at a quarter past 2.00 tomorrow in the same courtroom. Oh, no. I'm making a mistake. We're not sitting tomorrow. It's either age or time. Mr. Mandic, we're not sitting tomorrow. Tomorrow is a meeting of the Judges, a plenary meeting, so none of the Chambers will sit tomorrow. The day after tomorrow, a quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom. So that is the 9th of December. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Mandic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to turn into private session for just a second, and since we'll then adjourn for the day, those in the public gallery might not have a great interest in returning once they have left the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now in private session. One of the pending issues is the request to release the closed-session testimony of Milan Babic and the related exhibits under seal. The Chamber is willing to accommodate this request by the Defence, thus lifting the confidentiality on transcript pages on from 3323 to the end of this testimony, as well as all related exhibits. It will, however, formally do so only on the 31st of January of 2005. Since this allows the parties, as well as Mr. Babic himself, the opportunity to file further submissions on specific and objective elements showing the real likelihood of danger or risk still existing and that the Chamber should reconsider its willingness to proceed as it just said. The Chamber, therefore, kindly requests the registrar to convey this portion of the transcript to the Victims and Witness Section and to Mr. Babic. This is the issue I would like to deal with in private session. Perhaps we return now into open session.
